extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York / voters and delegates considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution (general public interested in constitutional principles)
extracted.subtask_description: A late-18th-century political-constitutional essay arguing for an indefinite federal power of taxation, the reasoning behind it, and responses to objections about representation, local knowledge, and abuses such as double taxation or poll taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to provide for future contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions of civil government must be framed not only on existing exigencies but also on probable future exigencies; government should have capacity to provide for future contingencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is fallacious to infer the extent of national power from immediate necessities; because future contingencies are illimitable, it is unsafe to attempt to strictly limit the federal government's capacity (examples: defense, naval wars, protecting commerce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite power to provide for emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the government must be able to guard against future invasions of public peace (foreign war or domestic convulsions), the power to provide for emergencies must be sufficiently broad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that attempts to limit the federal power of providing for emergencies would leave the government incapacitated in unforeseen crises; challenges critics to produce reliable data limiting such powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal taxation should not be confined to particular objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Restricting the national revenue jurisdiction to particular object(s) (e.g., only import duties) will produce undue proportional burdens and inequalities among industries, states, and citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two evils follow: oppression of particular branches of industry and unequal distribution of taxes among states and among citizens of the same state; limiting resources tempts over-reliance on narrow sources with harmful side effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import duties alone are an inadequate national fund
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying exclusively on duties on imports as the federal fund would be insufficient and unfair, producing inequality between manufacturing and non-manufacturing states and between consumers and merchants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exorbitant import duties encourage smuggling, premature monopolies for manufacturers, force industry into less advantageous channels, and sometimes fall on merchants rather than consumers; therefore import duties should be part of a broader revenue system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest of the revenue acts as a restraint on extreme taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: The general interest in preserving revenue will ordinarily guard against excessive duties, as long as other revenue avenues remain open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If other resources are closed, necessity may stimulate harmful experiments (e.g., extreme duties, regulatory overreach), so preserving multiple revenue sources is prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction of taxation (federal and state)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent jurisdiction in taxation was the only admissible substitute for total subordination of state authority; it reconciles indefinite federal taxation power with adequate and independent state resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent jurisdiction prevents sacrifice of Union interests to state power and allows states an independent power to provide for their own necessities while preserving federal capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid granting states exclusive revenue sources beyond their permanent needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Local governments should not command an exclusive source of revenue for any sum beyond what is reasonably necessary for their permanent expenses (e.g., modest civil lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting states exclusive control of significant revenue sources would divert community resources away from the Union and be unjustified; estimating permanent state needs (illustrated by 'about two hundred thousand pounds') should guide allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of taxation should not be tied to arbitrary separation of objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to repartition revenue objects between Union and states in proportion to comparative necessities is impractical because any specific fund will be either too great or too small for present and future wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives numerical illustration: leaving only external/internal lines would give states two-thirds of resources to meet a small fraction of expenses while the Union would have one-third to meet the majority, implying mismatch of means and ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative body need not include members of every occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impracticable and unnecessary to expect that every class (occupation) will have direct representatives; merchants, landholders, and learned professions will naturally represent wider classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics and manufacturers tend to vote for merchants who are their patrons; landholders share common interest on land taxes; learned professions act as impartial arbiters — so these groups will adequately represent other classes in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of representatives on constituents creates sympathy and information
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives, being dependent on suffrages and potentially bound by laws that affect themselves and their posterity, will have incentives to inform themselves of constituents' dispositions and to be sympathetic to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that electoral accountability motivates representatives to learn and reflect constituent interests; personal stakes bind them to consider public sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation requires extensive information best handled by capable statesmen or dedicated boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration and planning of public finances often commit to a few inquisitive and enlightened statesmen or boards who prepare tax plans later passed by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as evidence that a centralized or expert-driven approach to taxation is appropriate and feasible; local details are for execution, not necessarily policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: National legislature can obtain necessary local knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The national legislature can acquire knowledge of local circumstances (resources, agriculture, commerce, manufactures, property) from the representatives of each state; local detail execution is left to assessors/officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between minute topographical knowledge (not required) and general acquaintance with a state's situation and resources (sufficient for taxation decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of state systems and officers for tax collection to avoid duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Where practical, the federal government may employ state officers and adopt state collection systems to collect federal taxes, avoiding double sets of officers and minimizing expense and popular disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where objects are already regulated by states, federal use of existing state mechanisms is a practicable expedient; exclusive federal objects (e.g., import duties) are exceptions where duplication is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity requirement for duties, imposts, and excises
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a constitutional provision that 'all duties, imposts, and excises shall be uniform throughout the United States,' which helps guard against abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity plus apportionment by population are cited as legal safeguards against partiality or oppression in federal taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment by population as a guard against partiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions of internal taxes are to be determined by numbers of each state (census/enumeration), which effectively shuts the door to partiality or oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Census-based rules are presented as structural constraints limiting arbitrary taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between direct and indirect internal taxes and implications for administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal taxes may be direct (e.g., land taxes) or indirect (duties/excises); objections about local knowledge mainly apply to direct taxes, whereas indirect taxes are easier to understand and administer at the national level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct taxes' execution requires local assessors/commissioners; national law only needs to set qualifications and broad outlines. Indirect taxes are based on the nature of articles and merchant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections of double taxation are misplaced if federal collection replaces state collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Double taxation fears misunderstood: the community's tax burden will be similar whether taxes are raised by the union or states; federal collection can utilize import duties more prudently and reduce need for onerous internal taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the total quantity of taxes must be supplied one way or another; federal systems may better distribute burdens and leverage convenient revenue branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to levy poll taxes should exist though their use is objectionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Although poll taxes are disapproved of, the federal government should retain the option to use them in extraordinary national emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that possession of the power is not equivalent to its required exercise; extreme conjunctures might make poll taxes an essential resource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual abstinence and coordination to avoid policy interference between federal and state revenue laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid clashes in policy between federal and state revenue laws, each should mutually abstain from objects already occupied by the other; legal repugnancy is avoided but policy interference can be addressed by reciprocal forbearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When particular debts and state expenses are within natural compass, the possibility of interference diminishes; common immediate interests encourage cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most productive system of finance will be least burdensome (equity principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed, productive financial system will, by being efficient, impose the least burden on citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is used to argue that knowledgeable financiers and efficient federal arrangements will minimize oppressive measures and protect poorer classes.
